<reason>A offered the stronger comparative case: protect essential use, incentivize savings across discretionary uses, and retain restrictions for actual shortfalls. B raised credible concerns about price responsiveness and administering allowances, but repeatedly assumed that savings must come from vulnerable households despite A’s protections. B also failed to establish that retaining emergency restrictions makes them the primary instrument. A answered the pressure more directly and better distinguished recurring conservation policy from emergency intervention.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The decisive exchange was B’s preference for bans even if pricing met conservation targets while protecting essentials, followed by A’s distinction between price-sensitive discretionary consumption and essential consumption. B never justified its repeated claim that remaining wealthy lawns necessarily meant tenants and large families were supplying the savings.</best_rebuttal>
